consensus_summary: Consensus primary meaning of plural 'branches' is believers/disciples in living union with Christ the vine (John 15:1-8), deriving life and expected to bear fruit (with removal of fruitless ones); major common alternative is Romans 11 olive-tree branches as natural (Israel/Jews) and wild/grafted (Gentile) members of the covenant people; further alternatives include messianic singular 'Branch', palm branches of victory, tree branches as nations/kingdoms, and genealogical offspring.
book_summary: The members of a nation — broken off, or grafted in, while the tree itself stands (Rom 11:17; cross-ref Trees).
consensus_core_identification: People (believers or covenant members) attached to Christ/God as vine/root/tree, deriving spiritual life and subject to fruitfulness or removal/breaking.
book_core_identification: Members of a nation who may be broken off or grafted in, while the tree itself stands.
boundary_disagreement: Book restricts the symbol strictly to national members under the Romans 11 olive-tree image (broken/grafted while tree stands); consensus includes and usually prioritizes individual disciples as branches of the vine (John 15) plus other motifs, admitting a wider set of cases.
material_contradiction: None; the book's national olive-tree reading is already listed across the consensus responses as a common or primary alternative.
rationale: Minimum cores both identify branches as persons attached to a larger plant figure for God's people/Christ and subject to inclusion or exclusion. Book preserves that general category/referent but materially narrows extension, precision and primary focus to the national members of Romans 11 alone (excluding or de-emphasizing the dominant John 15 vine-discipleship sense and other alternatives), producing boundary refinement rather than core replacement, contradiction or novelty.
strongest_objection: Consensus treats John 15 as the most settled and prominent Christian use of plural 'branches,' so the book's exclusive elevation of the Romans 11 national sense may under-weight the dominant referent rather than merely refine its boundary.
